data.title: Precis Engineering + Architecture Hires Richert as Cary Director – Engineering Services
data.description:
AMBLER, N.C. —

Precis Engineering + Architecture, an award-winning design firm with offices in Ambler, Pa., and Cary, N.C., has hired G. Edward Richert, PE, LEED AP, as Director – Engineering Services in its Cary office. Ed Richert has 30+ years of pharmaceutical and biotechnology facility design and operations experience on both the owner/client and consulting engineering sides of the industry.

“Ed’s deep industry knowledge and perspective helps our clients better strategize, allowing us to arrive at thoughtful solutions that perform,” said Precis Principal – North Carolina Operations John McCullough, PE. “In addition to serving our clients, Ed is a talented leader-doer who provides important guidance and expertise to our growing team.”

As Director – Engineering Services, Richert operates as a technical resource to staff across all Precis disciplines, supports new business development, and oversees project deliverable quality controls.

“I’ve supported the biopharmaceutical community in the Research Triangle Park region for most of my career,” said Richert. “It feels especially fulfilling to join Precis, where leaders have hands-on involvement in every assignment. I’m excited to contribute to the innovative design solutions for which Precis is known and to foster long-term client relationships.”

Richert’s background includes sustainable capital project engineering design, energy management, strategic planning, product/process validation, and FDA design control implementation. His design experience spans utilities and infrastructure, laboratories, medical device facilities, active pharmaceutical ingredient plants, oral solid/liquid dosage facilities, sterile fill suites, and aseptic processing facilities.

Richert holds M.S. and B.S. in Engineering Science degrees from the University of Florida; is a registered professional engineer in 11 states; is a member of the American Society of Heating, Refrigeration, and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) and International Society for Pharmaceutical Engineering (ISPE); and is a lifetime supporting member of Tau Beta Pi. He lives with his family in Raleigh.

data.title: Most new drugs are still too costly at launch, ICER says
data.description:
Dive Brief:

  • The launch prices of two-thirds of the new prescription drugs reviewed by the watchdog group ICER between 2022 and 2025 far exceeded the organization’s threshold of cost-effectiveness, according to a report published Tuesday.
  • When adjusted for inflation, the median net price of new medicines spiked from $190,000 in 2022 to $257,000 in 2025, though most of that upswing occurred early on, ICER said. The 2025 figure includes high-cost gene and cell therapies that are expensive to manufacture but are often only administered once. Nearly a quarter of the drugs ICER evaluated last year had a net price surpassing $500,000.
  • ICER called on drugmakers to enact “fair pricing.” The group also pushed insurers to boost access to new therapies, noting that four in 10 prescriptions for the medicines it reviewed were rejected and that the statistics were worse for Medicare recipients. Value-based drug pricing should be “met with streamlined access to new drugs with little to no cost-sharing for patients,” ICER argued. 

Dive Insight:

Drug costs continue to be a hot-button topic in the U.S. The majority of Americans believe the price tags for prescription medicines are unreasonable and worry about being able to afford them, according to a recent poll from KFF.

Successive presidential administrations have sought to address this issue in one way or another. Former President Joe Biden signed into law a policy that, for the first time, gave Medicare the power to negotiate lower prices for certain drugs. Donald Trump has formed more than a dozen deals asking drugmakers to adopt “most-favored nation” prices in return for tariff relief. These moves have yet to meaningfully affect pharmaceutical companies’ bottom lines. 

The cost of medicines is a thorny issue for the pharmaceutical industry, which has long argued that drug innovation — a highly risky endeavor — requires a substantial return on investment to be worthwhile. ICER, or the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review, has for years aimed to provide a counter-voice, using a methodology that compares prices to the value medicines provide to argue costs should be lower. 

Drugmakers have contended that ICER’s cost-effectiveness guidelines, which take into account how medicines extend survival or improve quality of life, are flawed. Yet that framework is similar to what agencies in other countries, like the U.K.’s National Institute for Clinical Excellence, use to evaluate medicines. ICER’s benchmarks for value are $100,000 or $150,000 per “quality adjusted life year,” an academic measure of one year of perfect health.

ICER’s latest report drew statistics from the 26 drugs it previously reviewed and that were approved between 2022 and 2025. Of those medicines, Insmed’s lung-disease drug Brinsupri and Merck & Co.’s pulmonary arterial hypertension medicine Winrevair were judged to have the biggest disconnects between their net prices and overall value. ICER contended that both would need discounts of around 90% from their current costs to meet its guidelines.

Johnson & Johnson and Legend Biotech’s CAR-T therapy for multiple myeloma, Carvykti, could be reduced by one-third from its $465,000 net price to justify its cost, ICER said. 

Vertex Pharmaceuticals’ non-opioid pain drug Journavx, on the other hand, is priced within ICER’s cost-effectiveness thresholds. And Casgevy, the gene editing treatment from Vertex and partner CRISPR Therapeutics, might only need a 7% reduction from its $2.2 million net price to represent good value for money.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to clarify the current name of KFF.

data.title: Extractables in single-use systems used in ADC manufacturing
data.description:
Single‑use (SU) systems have great potential for use in antibody‑drug conjugate (ADC) manufacturing. The use of organic solvents in the ADC process might, however, raise questions about potential leachables from the plastic and elastomeric materials of single‑use components. To address those concerns, we performed extractables studies on a disposable chromatography column housing and two different disposable flow paths. The extractables studies were performed with two solvents commonly used in the ADC cytotoxin conjugation step: DMA and DMSO.

The studies were designed to ensure that conditions were exaggerated compared with existing ADC manufacturing processes. Extractable organic compounds and trace elements from the single‑use components were identified and semi‑quantitated with a complementary set of analytical techniques. The low levels of extractables found in this study support the use of ReadyToProcess™ columns, ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kits and ÄKTA ready™ flow kits in ADC processes.

Introduction

ADCs are biotherapeutic molecules consisting of a cytotoxin coupled to a monoclonal antibody (mAb) by a linker. The target specificity of the mAb enables delivery of the toxic drug to cancer cells, while minimizing collateral damage to healthy cells. mAbs used in ADC production are typically manufactured according to traditional processes, including purification via protein A‑platform processes (1, 2). Before coupling the linker, the mAb needs to be transferred to a suitable solution. This solvent exchange is normally performed by an ultrafiltration/diafiltration (UF/DF) operation. After the linker coupling reaction, the next step is the conjugation reaction, which couples the cytotoxic drug. Figure 1 provides an example workflow for manufacturing an ADC from a bulk mAb product. Conjugation reactions are typically performed in a solvent containing either N,N‑dimethylacetamide (DMA) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (3) at concentrations from 10% to 15%.

Fig 1. Simple workflow for preparing an ADC from bulk mAb.

SU systems are well suited to ADC manufacturing for several reasons. Importantly, SU systems minimize operator exposure to toxins, while also protecting the product from the operator and environment. The high potency of ADCs means that relatively small amounts of products need to be produced per batch. The small batch sizes are well suited for incorporation of SU technology, which provides a cost‑efficient solution for multi‑product manufacturing. In addition to the lower upfront capital cost compared with reusable systems, SU technologies are quicker to start using because they are supplied ready to use. Cleaning and cleaning validation between manufacturing campaigns is unnecessary and the risk of carryover of cytotoxin from one batch to another is minimized. Because cleaning is not performed, SU technologies minimize the volume of contaminated waste that must be handled and disposed of.

To support the adoption of SU technologies in ADC production, relevant extractables information is needed. Therefore, extractables studies were performed on three SU products: the ReadyToProcess™ 1 L column housing, disposable ÄKTA ready™ low flow kit for chromatographic systems and ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kit for tangential flow filtration (Fig 2 and 3).

Fig 2. ÄKTA ready™ system with a 20 L ReadyToProcess™ column and ÄKTA ready™ flow kit. In this study, 1 L column housings were used.
 

Fig 3. ÄKTA readyflux™ tangential flow filtration system with flow kit.

Materials and methods

The goal of the extraction studies was to characterize extractables profiles with equipment and conditions relevant to current ADC manufacturing processes. The studies were designed and performed with advice from customers who use disposables in their ADC processes.

Read about the study design, process, methods and analysis here

Results and discussion

ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kit

In the extract from the ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kit incubation, five organic compounds were found above reporting limit for each solvent (30% DMSO and 30% DMA). All compounds identities were assigned confirmed and the majority of them were related to antioxidants and silicone material. Some differences between the solvents could be seen, but the total amount of extractables found did not differ significantly. The compound with the highest abundance was a carboxylic acid, semi-quantified to 430 µg per ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kit.

For ICP-SFMS, the results were aligned between the solvents: four elements were above the reporting limit, the same elements in both solvents, with potassium having the highest abundance (3.8 mg/flow kit in 30% DMA).

ReadyToProcess™ column housings

No organic extractable compounds were found above the reporting limit with HS‑GC‑MS or GC‑MS in the extraction samples with 15% DMA or 15% DMSO. The results with LC‑MS showed one organic compound that was present in both 15% DMA and 15% DMSO. The extractable compound was assigned a confirmed identity level as an identified compound related to a curing agent used with elastomeric material. The concentration was estimated below 200 µg/L (ppb) in both extraction solvents (that is, less than 200 µg/ReadyToProcess™ column).

Analysis with ICP‑SFMS showed low levels of a few extractable elements. The most abundant were calcium (< 100 µg/L) and magnesium (< 25 µg/L), followed by zinc (< 10 µg/L) and barium (< 2 µg/L). The extractable elements were found at a similar level in both 15% DMA and 15% DMSO.

ÄKTA ready™ low flow kit

The results showed five organic extractable compounds above the reporting limit with HS‑GC‑MS, GC‑MS and LC‑MS. Two of the compounds were found in 15% DMA and three compounds were found in 15% DMSO. All five extractable compounds were assigned a confirmed identity level as identified compounds related to polyamide and silicone materials and one solvent. The highest abundant extractable compound was present at a concentration below 600 µg/L (that is, 410 µg/ ÄKTA ready™ low flow kit, because the extraction volume was 700 mL).

Analysis with ICP‑SFMS showed that the most abundant extractable element was silicon, which was present below 9 mg/L (ppm). Additionally, calcium, barium, zinc and copper were found at lower levels. The extractable elements were found at a similar level in both 15% DMA and 15% DMSO.

Assessment of results

A general toxicity and safety evaluation of extractable compounds as a worst case was conducted. The evaluation can only be general, because the specific details regarding the route of administration, dosage level, or toxicity of the proposed drug compounds will differ between different ADCs.

Toxicological information and a derived risk index (RI) for eight out of the ten identified extractable compounds were listed in a reference containing compiled safety impact information (4). In that reference, risk indices were obtained by subjecting toxicological safety data such as no observed effect levels (NOELs), no observed adverse effect levels (NOAELs), lowest published toxic dose (TDLOs) and others to a systematic evaluation process using appropriate uncertainty factors. An RI value represents a daily intake value for life‑long intravenous administration. Two additional RI values were derived for the final identified extractable compounds from a reported NOAEL value and appropriate uncertainty factors.

Assumptions for the assessment were:

  • Single‑use equipment included in this assessment comprise the column housing, the chromatography flow kit and the tangential flow filtration flow kit. All extractables from these disposables end up as impurity in the ADC product.
  • Batch size is 5 g, considered a small batch, representing a worst case.
  • Dosage is 3.6 mg/kg given every three weeks (21 d cycle), that is, 3.6 mg/kg × 70 kg bodyweight (bw)/21 d = 12 mg/person/d.

Potential exposure to extractables was calculated from the highest result on extractables divided with the batch size of ADC multiplied with the daily dosage of ADC (Table 6).

Assessment of the results according to the listed assumptions shows that the potential exposure to extractables is well below the RI for each extractable compound. Therefore, extractables from the ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kit, ReadyToProcess™ column housing and ÄKTA ready™ flow kit should pose no safety concern for use in ADC manufacturing within the conditions of this study.

Conclusions

The low levels of extractables found in this study demonstrate the chemical compatibility of ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kits, ReadyToProcess™ columns and ÄKTA ready™ flow kits with two organic solvents typically employed in ADC manufacturing processes: DMSO and DMA. Detailed results of these studies are available in the validation guides for these SU components to supplement existing data generated with aqueous solvents and ethanol. Along with other SU components and systems, the ÄKTA readyflux™ flow kits, ReadyToProcess™ columns and ÄKTA ready™ flow kits offer a solution to some of the main challenges in ADC manufacturing.

data.title: NeuroVista Labs Advances Neuroplasticity Drug Discovery Program with U.S. Market Focus
data.description:
CURITIBA, Brazil —

CURITIBA, Brazil, October 15, 2026 — NeuroVista Labs, a Brazilian biotechnology company developing a neuroplasticity-focused drug discovery program with the United States as its primary target market, today announced that its synthesized research compounds have advanced into in vitro testing in laboratories in Brazil.

The milestone moves the program from theoretical and computational research into experimental evaluation. The studies will investigate the compounds’ biological activity and generate evidence to guide subsequent development decisions.

Based in Curitiba, NeuroVista is conducting its research in Brazil while building a development strategy focused on the U.S. pharmaceutical market. The company aims to translate research conducted in Brazilian laboratories into drug development opportunities with international reach.

“We are building NeuroVista with a clear international direction: conducting research in Brazil while developing our program with the U.S. market as our primary focus,” said Ravi Kaiut, CEO and Lead Scientist of NeuroVista Labs. “Advancing from a hypothesis to synthesized compounds and laboratory testing gives us the opportunity to generate the experimental evidence needed to move that strategy forward.”

NeuroVista’s research focuses on neuroplasticity—the nervous system’s capacity to adapt and reorganize—as a foundation for investigating potential therapeutic approaches to neurological diseases.

The program began with a scientific hypothesis and computational research to inform compound design and selection. Following synthesis, the compounds are now undergoing in vitro evaluation in Brazil to assess whether their biological activity supports further development.

The program remains at an early stage of preclinical research. The compounds’ safety and efficacy in humans have not been established.

Media Contact

Ravi Kaiut | CEO and Lead Scientist

data.title: Iambic CEO on taking an AI drug company public
data.description:
The stock market, while broadly enthusiastic about artificial intelligence, hasn’t been as bullish on drug companies built around the technology.

Several of the AI-focused drug developers to go public so far have lost much of their market value. Shares of Exscientia, for example, had fallen roughly 80% from their debut price by the time the company agreed to sell to rival Recursion Pharmaceuticals in 2024. Recursion, too, has plummeted since initially listing shares at $18 apiece. Its stock price currently sits just under $4.

Iambic Therapeutics believes it will chart a different course. After launching in 2019, the AI specialist attracted close to half a billion dollars in funding from a list of prolific life sciences investors like Nexus, Abingworth and Catalio Capital Management. Iambic added to its cash pile earlier this week by raising $150 million through an IPO.

Iambic’s share price hovered around $24.50 by mid-Friday, up more than 50% from Wednesday. Whether this warmer embrace continues isn’t clear. Iambic's haul was well below what many of its biotech peers have drawn in from IPOs this year. It's also far less than some of the massive megarounds other AI-focused drugmakers have secured in the private markets. 

Tom Miller, Iambic’s co-founder and CEO, spoke to BioPharma Dive about his company’s IPO roadshow and what he sees as AI’s role in the future of drug development. The following conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

BIOPHARMA DIVE: How would you assess the track record of AI in drug discovery and development so far? What are its successes and what are the main challenges companies using it are facing?

MILLER: Iambic, since its founding, has really focused on bringing new molecules to and through clinical trials as our measure of success. When I think about execution in the AI space, I think about IAM1363 getting to the clinic in less than two years. I think about the fact that we're now poised to initiate registrational trials in 2027 because we have 100-plus patients worth of data that supports an aggressive and broad development plan. 

That's what every tech bio should be held up to. Technology is great. We should be asking: Are you converting it to medicines? 

That echoes some of the comments you made when Iambic announced its partnership with Takeda.

MILLER: That remains as true today as it was then. We're happy to stack up. 

The point of all of this technology, the point of any platform, is to execute on what comes off of it. Takeda gained a lot of conviction around our ability to do that. You see that more recently with the AbbVie deal as well [as] the Bayer deal. Pharma recognizes Iambic is a partner that can execute in that way.

Thus far there’ve been a few high profile companies — Recursion and Exiscentia come to mind — built around AI drug discovery that have struggled in the public markets. What lessons can you take from those experiences and what gives you confidence that your experience will be different?

MILLER: I'll just speak to what we have done at Iambic, and that is to make sure that by the time we reached the public markets, we had demonstrated compelling clinical data; we had multiple programs either in the clinic or [nearing human testing]; we had good and repeated demonstration of the underlying platform; but we also had enough tangible clinical data for people who aren't platform-forward to actually wrap their head around, to actually get conviction in. 

If you have a pure life science thesis, this is a company that excites you because of the medicines. If you have a pure tech thesis, this is a company that excites you because of the underlying technologies. And I think making sure that we build a company that can connect those dots and bring in that broader set of investors is an important part of our journey. 

What did you see from investors on your roadshow? Was there considerable skepticism? Many biotech IPOs this year have been bigger than this.

MILLER: Iambic came to the IPO with a very strong cash position on the basis of all of our partnerships. We announced at the end of the last quarter over $270 million of cash on hand — and that was prior to the AbbVie deal.

We sized the IPO and priced it with an eye towards bringing in a broad syndicate of investors who not only have understanding of what it takes to build great technology, but also have deep understanding on the life science side of what it takes to build great medicines. That sizing of the IPO has definitely been influenced by the cash efficiency of the company and the strong cash position of the company — the fact that we have more than we feel we need, to do what we need, in terms of reaching near-term inflection points.

Axios had a story earlier this week about a disconnect between how investors are looking at a company like yours versus others in the space. Isomorphic, according to a report, is in early talks to raise new funds at a valuation of at least $40 billion. Elsewhere, Chai Discovery recently secured $400 million in funding. Do you think investors are viewing the Iambic story differently than other AI drug developers?

MILLER: Iambic has been building a company that connects the thesis of better technologies making better medicines. We don't take a backseat on technology to anybody. 

What you see in terms of these partnership deals: we're happy to go AI model to AI model, we're happy to go partner to partner, with any company that you've mentioned or any other company that's out there. But we're also happy to go molecule to molecule in terms of real-world clinical development. 

If we're going to build a generational company that can operate with the innovation urgency of a tech company, but also with the execution maturity of a biotech, this is the approach that makes the most sense. 

There's been concerns that AI lends itself to hyperbolic statements. The CEO of Anthropic recently said the technology could cure all diseases within the next decade. What is your view of AI's eventual role? And, now that you’re public, do you anticipate having to change how you steer or position the company?

MILLER: If we keep our eye on the patient, if we keep our eye on the development of better medicines that have a genuine and urgent unmet need, then I think we are going to keep our eye on what really matters.

But Iambic’s focus has always been on the molecule being the important thing by which we're going to measure our success. That remains as true today as it ever was. 

Biotech investors, while maybe more optimistic than they were a few years ago, are also hyper-fixated on how companies are deploying their resources. How will you use this new IPO cash in a way that resonates with investors?

MILLER: I would just reiterate that Iambic has had roughly eight partnerships in the last roughly eight quarters. We've had a strong drumbeat of partnership activity. That has sustained us … and provides us with a very strong runway [to get to] clinical inflection points.

Your pipeline is currently composed of three cancer drugs. How do you evaluate whether to go deeper into oncology or diversify into other therapeutic areas? 

MILLER: You see in terms of our partnership announcements that Iambic is actively working in areas of neurology, in areas of inflammation and immunology, as well as in other therapeutic areas. We have a platform that is highly flexible across target class, across drug development modality and across therapeutic areas. 

Partnerships have given us a strong way to apply and validate our technology into more broad areas of drug development. To answer your question, this is allowing us to then feed back into our own wholly owned pipeline, [which], if you look deeper … extends beyond oncology. It includes metabolic disease. It includes endocrinology. Iambic is actively moving beyond oncology, despite the fact that we have a highly synergistic and focused trio of lead assets. 

How important do you think collaborations are for a company like yours moving forward, and maybe even the broader AI drug field? Is validation still one of the key benefits from a big pharma nod, or are we moving past that? 

MILLER: Iambic has never done it just for the logos on the slide. 

We had already validated that we could deliver our own molecules to the clinic. Any investor could just look at what we'd created and know that Iambic was for real in terms of drug development. We do these things because we think those partnerships make us stronger at our ability to develop our own wholly owned pipeline assets. 

We bring in additional staff onto our side that has expertise on those programs through the course of the partnerships. It makes us stronger in a lot of ways. It benefits the partner and it benefits us.

That's really what we're building.

data.title: Biotech M&A is accelerating. Track the deals that are happening here.
data.description:
In the business of drug development, deals can be just as important as scientific breakthroughs. Many of today's most lucrative medicines, from the life-saving cancer treatment Keytruda to the anti-inflammatory agent Enbrel, might not have become so without mergers and acquisitions.

The end of the last decade brought record highs in pharmaceutical M&A as larger companies turned again and again to young biotechs for innovation. Often, these deals focused on cancer, rare diseases and immune system disorders — areas of drug research that were seeing major victories in clinical trials and huge profits for treatments that made it to market.

2021 and 2022 were much quieter for dealmaking, as new challenges and then rising interest rates weighed on negotiations. But there have been signs of a rebound. Pharma companies are keen to expand in areas like obesity, while stocking up on newer technologies like antibody-drug conjugates. Even neuroscience, which large drugmakers previously abandoned, is drawing investment again.

BioPharma Dive is tracking M&A activity below. The database, which shows drugmaker buyouts that have happened since 2018 and were valued at $50 million or more in upfront consideration, will be regularly updated.

Click on an acquiring company to pull up more information, and scroll to the bottom of the page to read how this information was collected and organized. If there's anything we've missed, or any additional information you'd like to see, please reach out and let us know.

data.title: How early should you engage a CDMO?
data.description:
Bringing a new therapy into the clinic requires clinical, nonclinical, regulatory, and CMC activities to advance in parallel. In early development, getting drug in hand often sits on the critical path to toxicology studies and clinical trials, creating an understandable incentive to engage a CDMO and begin CMC work as early as possible.

But starting early and committing early are not the same thing.

Clinical, nonclinical, and CMC strategies are closely interconnected. Decisions about indication, dose, formulation, route of administration, nonclinical studies, and clinical trial design can influence what is ultimately required from the CMC program. When these workstreams are planned separately against an idealized timeline, CMC decisions can get ahead of the evidence needed to support them.

The result can be rework that costs both time and money.

When moving quickly creates work that has to be repeated

One development program shows how quickly those early assumptions can change.

A biotech company developing a poorly soluble API worked with its CDMO to address the solubility challenge, moving quickly to produce an engineering batch using a solubility-enhancement approach.

The work, however, was based on a preliminary target product profile and was completed before pharmacokinetic (PK) and toxicology studies were finalized.

Those studies changed the picture. The nonclinical results indicated that much lower doses, without solubility enhancement, would allow the company to evaluate safety and tolerability, characterize the PK profile in Phase I, and better inform the strategy and product attributes for Phase II.

The CMC work therefore had to be repeated using a non-solubilized approach. Rather than accelerating the program, the early formulation decision added cost and delayed both the IND filing and the start of the clinical trial.

The lesson is not that the company engaged its CDMO too early. It is that a product decision was advanced before the evidence needed to support it was available.

Engage early, but know what needs to remain flexible

Early CDMO engagement can be valuable, particularly when it helps development teams understand technical requirements, dependencies, timelines, and potential risks. But engaging early does not mean every element of the CMC strategy needs to be defined at the outset.

Drug substance development, for example, can often move forward while some drug product decisions remain open. This is particularly important when a program is considering multiple indications, since the indication ultimately pursued can affect dosing regimens, routes of administration, and other product requirements.

In one recent program, a biotech company developing an injectable API took a phase-appropriate approach to product supply for its first-in-human study. Rather than advancing process and scale development before longer-term nonclinical studies were complete, the team moved forward with fit-for-purpose clinical supply. This supported an earlier IND submission and trial start while allowing emerging nonclinical and clinical data to inform later development decisions. Once safety and tolerability were established, the team could advance process and scale development for resupply with greater confidence.

The goal is not to wait until every uncertainty has been resolved. It is to distinguish between activities that can move forward with confidence and decisions that depend on clinical or nonclinical evidence still being generated. Maintaining flexibility around those decisions can help avoid committing time and resources to work that may need to change as the development strategy takes shape.

Optimize the development plan, not one workstream

That flexibility matters because the goal is not to optimize CMC in isolation, but to keep CMC aligned with the needs of the broader development program.

A CDMO can play an important role in that process, helping translate laboratory processes into scalable drug substance and drug product strategies, define CMC scope and budgets, and plan for clinical supply. But those plans need to evolve alongside the clinical and nonclinical strategy as new data refine or challenge early assumptions.

That requires ongoing communication across CMC, clinical, nonclinical, and regulatory teams so that decisions made in one area continue to reflect what is being learned in others.

The objective is not to advance every CMC activity as quickly as possible. It is to advance the right activities at the right time, while preserving flexibility where important development questions remain unresolved.

A faster CMC timeline does not accelerate development if new evidence ultimately requires the work to be done again.

data.title: Biotech IPOs are the industry’s lifeblood. Track how they’re performing.
data.description:
Initial public offerings make the biotechnology industry tick. Stock listings give young companies the funding they need to develop their drugs, and their venture backers an opportunity to earn a return.

For much of the past decade, biotechs found Wall Street receptive to their pitches. Public investment, drawn in by scientific advances and company successes, bolstered generations of new drugmakers.

IPO activity reached a peak in 2021, when more than 100 biotechs priced an initial offering and together raised nearly $15 billion. But that momentum came to a halt in 2022 as stock prices of newly public companies plummeted amid a sector-wide downturn. The pace of IPOs stalled and, last year, only 11 drugmakers priced initial share sales.

Emerging biotechs now face a tougher road to public markets. Which will make it? Which create value and which fail? What types of companies earn the best returns? Who are their investors?

Biopharma Dive is tracking these questions in the database below, which will be updated regularly. If we've missed anything, or there's any additional information you'd like to see, please reach out and let us know.

data.title: Decreasing process variability in fluid management systems
data.description:
Connectivity represents something much larger than component compatibility. It is the foundation for standardization, predictability and control. Every connection influences whether a process can be reliably transferred, consistently executed and confidently scaled. When done right, early process decisions can translate to accelerated progress across development and scale‑up.

For organizations developing mAbs, mRNA therapies, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), multispecific antibodies and cell therapies—process robustness, technology transfer and manufacturing scalability increasingly rely on the effectiveness of single-use assemblies. Yet one factor remains consistently underestimated: physical connectivity or fluid management. The tubing, connectors, sensors and fluid transfer paths that link unit operations together can have a profound impact on flow behavior, process consistency, scalability and regulatory compliance.

As therapies become more complex and manufacturing networks expand across sites, every connection point in a process becomes a potential source of variability. These connectors are not merely passive components. Together, they define how material moves through a process, how consistently the process performs and how easily it can be transferred, replicated and scaled.

The challenge is that bioprocesses may evolve over time based on modality-specific requirements, which means incorporating new equipment or retrofitting technologies. A straightforward process can then become a patchwork of connection types, tubing dimensions, materials and supplier specifications. As manufacturers document deviations and are forced to troubleshoot flow inconsistencies and validate component changes, they’re left repeatedly asking the question, Why does this process behave differently here than it did there?

Physical connectivity is not simply about ensuring components fit together, it’s ensuring that the entire manufacturing system functions together. The performance of a process is influenced not just by a connector, tubing segment or flow kit, but by how all the elements of the fluid pathway interact as an integrated system. Small decisions made upstream can have significant consequences downstream. In this article, we discuss a few examples of why connectors can’t be chosen with only one piece of the process in mind.

End-to-end fluid management: why flow kits can’t be designed in isolation

In modern biomanufacturing, every transfer step must behave as expected. Unexpected flow behavior can result in batch delays, troubleshooting efforts, product loss or deviations that impact manufacturing efficiency. Yet flow path design decisions are often evaluated at the equipment level rather than at the process level. Because fluids do not recognize equipment boundaries, the performance of a flow kit is influenced by the entire transfer system surrounding it. Designing flow kits in isolation can therefore create hidden risks that are not discovered until the process is operating under real manufacturing conditions.

A common misconception in bioprocessing is that a flow kit can be designed around the requirements of the processing unit alone. The entire fluid transfer pathway within this skid, from the origin through the flow kit and to the destination, must be considered. Take, for example, a chromatography skid with a flow kit designed around a bore size of “X.” In chromatography, bore size refers to the internal diameter (ID) of the tubing. At first glance, it may seem reasonable to use X as the bore size through the system. However, many manufacturing facilities operate with long transfer distances between buffer preparation areas and process skids. Over those distances, pressure losses can become significant.

In these cases, MSAT and process engineers may intentionally specify a bore size larger than X, even though this is larger than the bore of the system flow path itself. The larger tubing diameter helps reduce pressure drop across long runs, minimizing the risk of cavitation, tubing collapse, pump performance issues and process interruptions.

A successful design requires consideration of the entire transfer pathway, including:

  • Mixer bag and tote outlet sizes
  • Tubing diameters across transfer distances
  • Transfer set configurations
  • Pump requirements
  • Pressure-drop limitations
  • Aseptic connector sizing
  • Final flow kit geometry

What appears to be a simple tubing selection decision is often a system-level engineering decision. For organizations seeking predictable manufacturing performance, every connection point must be considered within the context of the complete process. A well-designed fluid management strategy accounts not only for the flow kit itself, but also for the entire network of components that deliver fluid to and from the process (Fig 1).

Many connectivity challenges are not discovered when a component is selected. They are discovered during scale-up, technology transfer or commercial manufacturing. Cytiva works alongside you to design, evaluate and optimize manufacturing systems with the goal of reducing complexity, improving standardization and creating more robust processes from development through commercial production. data.title: Integra Therapeutics strengthens executive leadership with the appointment of Simon Dew as Chief Business Officer
data.description:
BARCELONA, Spain —

Integra Therapeutics, a global leader in cutting-edge gene writing tools designed to improve the efficacy, precision and safety of advanced therapies, today announced the appointment of Simon Dew as Chief Business Officer (CBO). 

Mr. Dew brings extensive executive experience in business development and licensing, corporate strategy, portfolio planning, commercial development, alliance management, and investor relations. He joins Integra from Macomics Ltd., where he was responsible for developing and implementing a business plan for out licensing clinical assets and platform technology with the primary purpose of partnerships within biopharma and academia.

Previously, Mr. Dew served as Chief Business Officer at ReNeuron Plc; Vice President of Business and Corporate Development at Mereo BioPharma; Vice President of Business Development at Evox Therapeutics; Vice President of Corporate Strategy at Gyroscope Therapeutics (acquired by Novartis); and SVP Corporate Strategy and Communications at Astellas Pharma. Earlier in his career, he held positions as Project Director at GSK and Product Manager at Bristol Myers.

Mr. Dew completed an Executive Leadership Program at Duke University and holds a BSc in Pharmacy from the University of Portsmouth. He is a member of the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain.

“We are delighted to welcome Simon to our leadership team at such a pivotal time for Integra. His vast experience in business development and corporate strategy across cell and gene therapy, oncology, immunology, and rare diseases will be crucial as we enter our next phase of growth, building alliances with global industry leaders to maximize the reach and value of FiCAT,” said Avencia Sanchez-Mejias, PhD, CEO & Co-Founder of Integra Therapeutics.

“Integra has built a highly differentiated gene writing modular platform with the potential to improve the precision and scalability of cell engineering for next-generation CAR-T therapies,” said Mr. Dew. “The opportunity to help address some of the major limitations of current treatments, including severe toxicities, high costs, and manufacturing delays, is only the beginning. I’m thrilled to join Integra at this exciting stage and and to work with the team to build the partnerships that will bring FiCAT's potential to patients.’’

FiCAT platform for next-generation CAR-T therapies

FiCAT (Find‑Cut‑And‑Transfer) is a next generation gene writing platform developed by Integra Therapeutics that enables precise, efficient, stable insertion of DNA fragments of unparalleled size into a genome, in a single step without viral vectors dependancies. It combines a ‘find’ module based on CRISPR‑Cas to target a specific genomic site, with a ‘cut‑and‑transfer’ module derived from a engineered transposase to insert the new genetic material in ex vivo and in vivo cell therapy (CAR-T) and gene therapy. FiCAT can be delivered in a viral-free manner via LNP pre-loading, with demonstrated efficiency in several tissues and cells. It is currently in preclinical development for oncology, autoimmune and genetic diseases.
